whoIsThisFor.heading: Who should take the MuleSoft Integration Architect exam?

personas.label: Senior integration consultants
personas.description: You have built Mule applications and now design complete integration solutions for customers.

personas.label: Enterprise architects
personas.description: You decide how systems connect and how the integration platform meets security, availability, and operational needs.

personas.label: Technical leads
personas.description: You guide MuleSoft teams and need to explain decisions about reliability, performance, and deployment.

examDifficulty.heading: How challenging is the MuleSoft Integration Architect exam?
examDifficulty.summary: The exam asks you to choose designs that meet both business needs and technical constraints. Questions often turn on reliability, latency, data volume, security, and where applications must run.
bullets: 60 scored questions in 120 minutes, plus up to five unscored questions that do not count.
70% to pass, which is 42 correct answers out of 60.
Architecture reasoning: Be ready to compare patterns against availability, performance, scale, and security requirements.
Broad platform scope: Review API-led design, deployment, messaging, transactions, monitoring, and governance.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: Practice designing integrations from a set of requirements. For each design, explain expected failure behavior, data flow, security, and runtime placement. Aim for at least 80% on practice questions and review any trade-off you cannot justify.

examFormat.heading: MuleSoft Integration Architect exam format
examFormat.intro: The exam is proctored online. Questions describe business and technical integration requirements.
examFormat.scenarioPercent: Most questions use scenarios, such as a requirement to avoid message loss during an outage or to process a large data volume within a defined window.
bestWayToPass: Read for constraints: Notice requirements such as guaranteed delivery, low latency, on-premises hosting, or high throughput.
Compare deployment models: Review CloudHub, Runtime Fabric, and customer-hosted runtimes.
Plan for reliability: Understand queues, transactions, idempotency, retries, and dead-letter handling.
Apply API-led layers: Put system access, cross-system business logic, and consumer-specific shaping in the appropriate APIs.

certificationCard.description: This exam covers MuleSoft integration architecture, including API-led layers, runtime deployment, reliability, performance, security, and governance. The guide allows up to five additional unscored questions. The exam is 60 scored questions in 120 minutes, with a 70% pass mark, weighted towards Designing for the runtime plane technology architecture and Designing and developing Mule applications (15% each).

blocks.heading: Integration Patterns and Delivery Guarantees
blocks.body: Use synchronous request and reply when the caller needs an immediate answer. Asynchronous queues can buffer messages when the caller can continue or the target system may be unavailable. Batch processing handles large scheduled data sets. Publish and subscribe can distribute events to multiple consumers. Scatter-Gather calls independent routes in parallel and combines their results. Each choice has a cost: queues add processing delay but can protect work during an outage, while synchronous calls are direct but depend on the target being available.

blocks.heading: API-Led Connectivity
blocks.body: System APIs provide controlled access to systems of record. Process APIs combine data and apply business rules across systems. Experience APIs shape responses for a specific app or channel. This separation can support reuse and reduce coupling. Put logic in the layer that owns the responsibility and avoid copying the same transformation into every consumer.

blocks.heading: Reliability, Transactions, and Idempotency
blocks.body: Choose a delivery approach that matches the required guarantee. Queues can persist messages until a consumer processes them. Transactions coordinate operations that must succeed or roll back together when the participating resources support the transaction. Idempotency prevents a repeated request from creating duplicate effects, often by tracking an identifier in an Object Store or using a unique key. Retries should be bounded and failed messages should be visible for recovery.

blocks.heading: Deployment and Runtime Architecture
blocks.body: Select where Mule applications run based on network, security, availability, scale, and operational requirements. CloudHub provides managed cloud runtimes. Runtime Fabric supports deployment to customer-managed infrastructure such as Kubernetes while allowing Anypoint Platform management. Customer-hosted runtimes may suit other environments. Design for redundancy and understand how clustered deployments coordinate scheduled work.

blocks.heading: Security, Governance, and Operations
blocks.body: Protect credentials through secure properties or a managed credential mechanism; never hard-code secrets. API Manager policies can enforce client identity, rate limits, and other controls. Governance and Exchange help teams apply standards and reuse APIs. Monitoring alerts can notify operators when error rates or other measures exceed thresholds. Include dashboards, alerts, and runbooks in the design.

scenarioTips.h2: How to prepare for the MuleSoft Integration Architect exam
scenarioTips.intro: Identify the requirement that rules out otherwise workable designs. Compare latency, throughput, delivery guarantees, runtime location, and operations.

blocks.heading: Choose the API-Led Layer
blocks.body: Use a System API for a system of record, a Process API for cross-system logic, and an Experience API for a specific consumer.

blocks.heading: Design for Reliability
blocks.body: Use durable messaging when work must survive outages. Add idempotency, bounded retries, and a dead-letter path for failures.

blocks.heading: Match Runtime to Constraints
blocks.body: Compare managed cloud, Runtime Fabric, and customer-hosted options based on security, network access, operations, and availability.

blocks.heading: Secure and Govern APIs
blocks.body: Use API Manager policies for client controls and rate limiting. Store credentials securely and publish reusable assets with clear standards.

blocks.heading: Monitor the Solution
blocks.body: Define operational measures and alerts before release. Make sure teams can see failures and know how to recover work.

nextCertsAfter.heading: Related credentials for MuleSoft integration architects
nextCertsAfter.intro: Continue with a MuleSoft developer, platform, or Salesforce integration architecture credential.

sampleQuestions.question: Orders must be preserved while the ERP is unavailable for an hour. Which design best supports this?
options: Keep orders in volatile memory until the ERP returns
Queue the orders and process them when the ERP is available
Call the ERP synchronously and discard orders on error
Drop failed orders and ask customers to resubmit
sampleQuestions.explanation: A durable queue can hold orders while the ERP is down and deliver them after service recovers.
whyWrong: Volatile memory may be lost if the runtime restarts during the outage.
A queue can preserve orders until the ERP is available.
A synchronous call that fails does not preserve the order.

sampleQuestions.question: Customer data from SAP, Salesforce, and billing must be combined for several applications. Where should that shared business logic live?
options: In a separate Experience API for each app
sampleQuestions.explanation: A Process API can combine data from several systems and expose reusable business logic to multiple consumers.
whyWrong: An Experience API shapes data for one consumer rather than combining shared business logic.
A Process API can combine systems for multiple consumers.
A System API should focus on access to one source system.

sampleQuestions.question: A retried payment message could otherwise charge a customer twice. What should the design use?
sampleQuestions.explanation: An idempotency check can recognize a repeated request and prevent a second payment effect.
whyWrong: Worker size does not prevent a duplicate payment.
A longer timeout cannot identify a repeated request.
Idempotency can detect a repeat and prevent a second charge.

sampleQuestions.question: A bank requires Mule workers to run on its own Kubernetes clusters so its infrastructure controls remain in force. Which deployment option fits?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Runtime Fabric places the Mule runtime on customer-managed Kubernetes infrastructure while keeping it connected to Anypoint management.
whyWrong: Studio is a development tool, not the managed customer Kubernetes runtime.
Runtime Fabric supports Anypoint-managed apps on customer infrastructure.
CloudHub is MuleSoft-managed hosting rather than the stated on-premises option.

sampleQuestions.question: A database update and a JMS message must either both succeed or both roll back. What should the architect consider?
sampleQuestions.explanation: A supported XA transaction can coordinate participating resources so the operations commit or roll back together.
whyWrong: Batch processing handles records but does not make two resource updates atomic.
Retries do not guarantee both resources commit or roll back together.
A supported XA transaction coordinates both resources.

sampleQuestions.question: One partner is sending so many requests that other API consumers are slowed. What control should be applied?
options: Move the API to a batch job
Apply a rate-limiting policy in API Manager
Increase worker size for all consumers
sampleQuestions.explanation: A rate-limiting policy can restrict request volume so one consumer does not overwhelm the API.
whyWrong: Removing all access is broader than necessary.
Batch processing changes the data exchange pattern rather than limiting one consumer.
Rate limiting controls request volume for an API or consumer.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the main purpose of a Center for Enablement?
options: Build every API centrally for all teams
sampleQuestions.explanation: A C4E enables teams to discover and reuse assets and follow shared standards.
whyWrong: A C4E helps teams discover and reuse APIs through shared practices.
Security remains a separate organizational responsibility.
Manual approval of every change can turn enablement into a bottleneck.

sampleQuestions.question: An application must call three systems in parallel and combine the responses before returning. Which Mule scope fits?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Scatter-Gather runs routes in parallel and aggregates their responses.
whyWrong: Scatter-Gather runs parallel routes and combines their results.
Choice routes messages by conditions rather than parallelizing calls.
Until Successful retries an operation but does not combine route responses.

sampleQuestions.question: Ten million records must move from a database to a warehouse overnight. What is a suitable approach?
options: A synchronous API call for each record
Load all records into memory in one flow
sampleQuestions.explanation: Batch processing can handle large data sets as records in controlled steps.
whyWrong: Synchronous per-record requests are inefficient at this volume.
Manual transfer is not a dependable nightly integration.
Batch jobs process large sets in manageable records or groups.

sampleQuestions.question: Where should a Mule application’s passwords and API keys be stored?
options: In the flow XML as constants
In plain-text properties committed to source control
In an API description in Exchange
In encrypted secure properties or a managed credential store
sampleQuestions.explanation: Encrypted secure properties or managed credentials protect secrets from exposure in application source.
whyWrong: Hard-coded credentials can be exposed in source code.
Plain-text properties in source control are not a secure secret store.
Exchange descriptions are not a credential vault.

sampleQuestions.question: How can a Mule cluster provide failover while avoiding duplicate execution of a scheduled job?
options: Run the scheduler on every server
sampleQuestions.explanation: Use a clustered deployment for redundancy and configure the scheduler to run on the primary node, so only one cluster member executes the task.
whyWrong: A cluster supports failover, with scheduling configured to run only on the primary node.
More memory does not remove the single-server failure risk.
Independent nodes without coordination can duplicate scheduled work.

sampleQuestions.question: Existing System and Process APIs expose order data. Which API should provide the mobile app with a focused order view for its small-screen workflow?
options: A new System API to the ERP
A copy of the Process API for each phone
Direct database access from the app
An Experience API for the mobile app
sampleQuestions.explanation: An Experience API can tailor the existing business data and contract to a particular consumer such as the mobile app.
whyWrong: A System API provides access to the ERP rather than tailoring the mobile response.
Copying the Process API creates duplicate logic.
Direct database access bypasses the existing API design.

sampleQuestions.question: Messages that still fail after bounded retries must be reviewed without blocking the queue. What should be used?
sampleQuestions.explanation: A dead-letter queue holds messages that failed processing so they can be inspected and handled separately.
whyWrong: Infinite retries can block the queue and overload a failing system.
Deleting failed messages loses work that may need review.
A larger queue does not separate repeatedly failing messages for inspection.

sampleQuestions.question: An API should accept calls only from registered applications presenting valid client credentials. What should be applied?
options: Restrict calls to approved network IPs
sampleQuestions.explanation: Client ID enforcement requires registered clients to present their client credentials.
whyWrong: Caching does not verify which application is calling.
Client ID enforcement validates registered client credentials.
Worker size does not authenticate API consumers.

sampleQuestions.question: The team wants an alert when an API’s error rate exceeds five percent. What should it configure?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Anypoint Monitoring alerts can notify operators when a configured error-rate threshold is exceeded.
whyWrong: Monitoring alerts can notify the team when a threshold is crossed.
A weekly report may miss an issue that needs immediate response.
Manual review does not automatically alert on a rate threshold.
